claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection of single-phase noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles with more than five elements are governed primarily by configurational entropy and relative atomic-size mismatch.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch beyond a critical threshold destabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Exceeding the critical atomic-size-mismatch threshold promotes phase separation.
Exceeding the critical atomic-size-mismatch threshold promotes elemental segregation.
The destabilizing effect of excessive atomic-size mismatch occurs regardless of rapid heating and cooling rates.
Atomic-size mismatch can be quantified using the variance in atomic radii among the constituent elements.
High configurational entropy favors formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Excessive atomic-size mismatch increases lattice-strain energy.
Lattice-strain energy generated by excessive atomic-size mismatch can overcome configurational-entropy stabilization.
Overcoming configurational-entropy stabilization drives phase separation or elemental segregation.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch beyond a critical value decreases the probability of obtaining a single-phase solid solution.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch beyond a critical value increases non-uniform particle morphology.
Below the atomic-size-mismatch threshold, a single-phase solid solution is maintained.
Low-mismatch nanoparticles at the stated baseline form a single-phase solid solution.
The hypothesis applies to noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements under rapid heating and cooling.
The hypothesis does not apply to systems containing fewer elements.
The hypothesis does not apply under slow thermal processing.
The critical atomic-size-mismatch threshold is system-dependent.
Electronic effects may also influence phase formation or crystal-structure selection.
Surface energies may also influence phase formation or crystal-structure selection.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention require atomic-size mismatch to change at fixed composition, but the proposed manipulation substitutes different elements. Elemental substitution changes the chemical composition, even if elemental fractions or total atom count are held constant.
